title: Imports and Namespace Setup
content: Imports Mathlib modules for finite sets (`Finset.Basic`, `Finset.Card`, `Finset.Interval`), natural number intervals (`Nat.Interval`, `Interval.Finset.Nat`), big operator notation (`BigOperators`), and real numbers (`Data.Real.Basic`). Opens `Finset` and `BigOperators` namespaces for concise notation. The `Erdos867` namespace scopes all definitions.
mathContext: Uses `Finset.Ioc` for the half-open interval $(a, b] \cap \mathbb{N}$, `Finset.Icc` for $[a, b] \cap \mathbb{N}$, `List.sum` for $\sum_{i} a_i$, and `Nat.log2` for $\lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor$. The `BigOperators` import enables `\sum` notation.

title: Consecutive Sums Definition
content: Defines `consecutiveSums : List N -> Finset N` collecting all sums of consecutive subsequences. For a sorted list A = [a_1, ..., a_t], it computes all sums a_i + a_{i+1} + ... + a_j for 0 <= i and j < |A|. Implementation uses nested folds over `List.range`, with `List.drop i` and `List.take (j+1)` to extract segments, then `List.sum` to compute each sum.
mathContext: For $A = [a_1, \ldots, a_t]$, the set of consecutive sums is $\{\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k : 0 \leq i \leq j < t\}$. This includes single elements ($i = j$). The total number of consecutive sums is $\binom{t+1}{2}$, though many may coincide.

title: Consecutive Sum-Free Property
content: Defines `isConsecutiveSumFree : List N -> Prop` requiring that for all indices i < j with segment length > 1, the sum of the segment A[i..j] does not lie in A.toFinset. The length > 1 condition excludes single-element 'sums' (trivially in A). This is the central predicate: A is consecutive sum-free iff no genuine consecutive sum lands back in A.
mathContext: A set $A = \{a_1 < \cdots < a_t\}$ is consecutive sum-free if $\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k \notin A$ for all $i < j$. Equivalently, $A \cap \text{consecutiveSums}(A) \setminus A = \emptyset$ when restricting to multi-element sums. This generalizes the classical sum-free condition $A \cap (A + A) = \emptyset$.

title: Maximum Density Function
content: Defines `maxDensity : N -> R` as the supremum of |A|/N over all lists A. Marked noncomputable since it uses `sSup` (completeness of reals). This is a simplified definition; the full version would constrain A to be a sorted subset of {1, ..., N} that is consecutive sum-free.
mathContext: The maximum density $\mu(N) = \sup\{|A|/N : A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\},\, A \text{ consecutive sum-free}\}$. Erdős conjectured $\mu(N) \leq 1/2 + O(1/N)$. The actual value satisfies $13/24 \leq \limsup \mu(N) \leq 2/3 - 1/512$.

title: Upper Half Construction
content: Defines `upperHalf N = Finset.Ioc (N/2) N`, the set of natural numbers in the half-open interval (N/2, N]. For N = 10, this gives {6, 7, 8, 9, 10}. This is the canonical example achieving density 1/2: any two elements a, b > N/2 satisfy a + b > N, so no sum of consecutive elements can lie in {1, ..., N}.
mathContext: The upper half $A = (\lfloor N/2 \rfloor, N] \cap \mathbb{N}$ has $|A| = N - \lfloor N/2 \rfloor = \lceil N/2 \rceil$. For any $a, b \in A$ with $a \neq b$, $a + b > N$, so $a + b \notin \{1, \ldots, N\} \supseteq A$. This is the largest 'obvious' consecutive sum-free set.

title: Upper Half Cardinality (PROVED)
content: Proves `upperHalf_card : (upperHalf N).card = N - N/2` by simplifying with `Finset.card_Ioc`. This is a genuine Lean proof using the Mathlib lemma that `|Ioc a b| = b - a` for natural numbers. For even N, this gives exactly N/2; for odd N, it gives (N+1)/2.
mathContext: $(\text{Ioc}\,(N/2)\,N).\text{card} = N - \lfloor N/2 \rfloor$. By `Finset.card_Ioc`: $|\{a+1, \ldots, b\}| = b - a$ when $a \leq b$. Since $\lfloor N/2 \rfloor \leq N$, the result follows.

title: Upper Half Density and Sum-Free Property
content: Two axiomatized properties: (1) `upperHalf_density`: for N >= 2, |upperHalf(N)| >= N/2 - 1, confirming density approaches 1/2. (2) `upperHalf_sumFree`: for N >= 4 and distinct a, b in upperHalf(N), a + b > N. The sum-free property follows because any consecutive sum of 2+ elements exceeds N and thus cannot lie in {1, ..., N}.
mathContext: For $a, b \in (N/2, N]$ with $a \neq b$: $a + b > 2 \cdot (N/2) = N$. More generally, $\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k \geq 2 \cdot (N/2 + 1) > N$ for $j > i$, so $\text{upperHalf}(N)$ is consecutive sum-free.

title: Adenwalla's Dyadic Upper Bound
content: Axiomatizes two results: (1) The dyadic lemma: if |A intersect [x, 2x]| = t, then the t-1 consecutive pair sums land in (2x, 4x] and are forbidden, giving |A intersect [x, 4x]| <= t + 2x - t + 1 = 2x + 1. (2) The global bound: |A| <= (2/3)N + log_2(N) + 1 for any consecutive sum-free A in {1, ..., N}. The O(log N) term comes from summing over O(log N) dyadic intervals.
mathContext: Partition $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ into $\sim \log_2 N$ dyadic intervals $[2^k, 2^{k+1})$. In each pair of adjacent intervals $[2^k, 2^{k+2})$: if $t$ elements lie in $[2^k, 2^{k+1})$, the $t-1$ pair sums are distinct and lie in $(2^{k+1}, 2^{k+2}]$. So $|A \cap [2^k, 2^{k+2})| \leq 2^{k+1} + 1$, giving density $\leq 2/3 + O(1/2^k)$.

title: Freud's Construction (1993)
content: Axiomatizes Freud's 1993 disproof: there exists a function f : N -> List N such that for all N >= 36, f(N) is a sorted subset of {1, ..., N}, is consecutive sum-free, and has |f(N)| * 36 >= 19 * N - 36, achieving density >= 19/36 ~ 0.5278. This is the key counterexample to Erdős's conjecture, published in the James Cook Mathematical Notes.
mathContext: Freud constructed explicit sets $A_N \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ with $|A_N| \geq \frac{19}{36}N - O(1)$. The integer arithmetic $|A| \cdot 36 \geq 19N - 36$ avoids rational division. Since $19/36 > 1/2$, this disproves $|A| \leq N/2 + O(1)$.

title: 19/36 > 1/2 (PROVED)
content: Proves `nineteen_thirty_sixth_gt_half : (19 : Q) / 36 > 1 / 2` via `norm_num`. This single line formally verifies that Freud's density exceeds the conjectured threshold, completing the disproof. The `norm_num` tactic handles rational arithmetic automatically.
mathContext: $\frac{19}{36} = 0.527\overline{7} > 0.5 = \frac{1}{2}$. Equivalently, $19 \cdot 2 = 38 > 36 = 36 \cdot 1$. This is the critical numerical fact that turns Freud's construction into a formal disproof.

title: Coppersmith-Phillips Bounds (1996)
content: Axiomatizes the state-of-the-art bounds from SIAM J. Discrete Math: (1) Lower: for N >= 24, there exists A in {1, ..., N} with |A| * 24 >= 13 * N - 24, achieving density >= 13/24 ~ 0.5417. (2) Upper: for any consecutive sum-free A in {1, ..., N}, |A| * 512 * 3 <= (2*512 - 3) * N + 512 * 3 * log_2(N), giving density <= 2/3 - 1/512 ~ 0.6647. The integer formulations avoid rational arithmetic in the axiom statements.

title: Bounds Consistency (PROVED)
content: Proves `best_bounds_fractions : (13 : Q) / 24 < 2/3 - 1/512` via `norm_num`. This verifies that the lower bound 13/24 is strictly less than the upper bound 2/3 - 1/512, confirming the Coppersmith-Phillips bounds are consistent (there is a genuine gap between them).

title: Connection to Problem 839 (Infinite Version)
content: Defines `isInfiniteConsecutiveSumFree : Set N -> Prop` for infinite sets: for every list of length >= 2 that is strictly increasing with all terms in A, the sum is not in A. Axiomatizes `problem_839_connection`: the asymptotic density of any infinite consecutive sum-free set is at most 2/3. Problem #839 is the infinite analogue of #867.
mathContext: Problem #839 asks: what is the supremum of the upper asymptotic density $\bar{d}(A) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} |A \cap [1, N]|/N$ over all infinite consecutive sum-free sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$? The $2/3$ upper bound carries over from the finite setting.

title: Concrete Examples (PROVED)
content: Three computationally verified examples: (1) {3, 4, 5} is a subset of Icc 1 5, proved via `simp` and `omega`. (2) |{3, 4, 5}| = 3, proved via `native_decide`. (3) {6, 7, 8, 9, 10} = upperHalf 10, proved via `ext`, `simp`, and `omega`. These demonstrate the definitions work correctly on small inputs. The set {3, 4, 5} achieves density 3/5 = 0.6, exceeding both 1/2 and 13/24.

title: Erdős's Conjecture is False
content: Axiomatizes `erdos_867_conjecture_false`: the negation of the claim that for all N >= 2 and all A in {1, ..., N} with the required properties, |A| * 2 <= N + 2. This is axiomatized because the full proof requires exhibiting Freud's explicit construction and verifying its consecutive sum-free property.
mathContext: The axiom states $\neg(\forall N \geq 2,\, \forall A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\},\, |A| \cdot 2 \leq N + 2)$. The witness is Freud's construction with $|A| \geq (19/36)N - O(1)$, giving $|A| \cdot 2 \geq (19/18)N - O(1) > N + 2$ for large $N$.
